## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 87, titled *Mañcapīṭha*, sets out the monastic disciplinary rule governing the construction of beds and benches [SuttaCentral]. Under this rule, a monk who constructs a bed with excessively long legs must shorten the legs to the permitted standard and confess the expiation-worthy offense (*pācittiya*) [SuttaCentral; Radich 2007]. It is categorized as a *chedanaka-pācittiya* rule, requiring physical alteration or excision of the illicit item in addition to formal confession [Hüsken 1997]. The *Samantapāsādikā* commentary discusses the practical application of this requirement, noting that if one does not wish to cut down the legs, sinking them into the ground to the proper measurement is also considered allowable [Hüsken 1997].

Scholars observe that Pācittiya 87 directly reflects the ethical restraint against using high or luxurious beds (*uccāsayanamahāsayanā veramaṇī*), an ascetic principle found throughout the Vinaya and early ethical codes [Keown 1992; Hüsken 1997]. Michael Radich points out that together with neighboring provisions on luxurious needlecases (Pācittiya 86) and upholstered furniture (Pācittiya 88), this rule regulates the material disposition and physical comportment of monastics [Radich 2007]. Ute Hüsken further notes that the non-offense (*anāpatti*) formula in Pācittiya 87 presents an abbreviated casuistry in comparison with other *chedanaka* rules [Hüsken 1997].

The rule has an exact counterpart in the nun's code as Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 163, as well as extensive parallels across all surviving Vinaya lineages, including the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsaṅghika, Dharmaguptaka, and Kāśyapīya traditions preserved in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan [SuttaCentral]. In text-reuse analysis, DharmaNexus records widespread formulaic overlap with neighboring Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga sections (especially Pācittiyas 88–92, Saṅghādisesas 6–7, and Nissaggiya Pācittiyas 13–15), as well as computational cross-linguistic alignments with Sanskrit and Tibetan Bhikṣuṇīvinaya texts [DharmaNexus].
